segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Masters, give your slaves what is just and fair, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Persevere in prayer, keeping alert in it with thanksgiving,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and pray for us as well, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the secret of Christ, for which I am in chains,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that I may make it plain, as I ought to speak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Walk in wisdom toward those outside, making the most of the time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you know how you ought to answer each person.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Tychicus will tell you all about how things are with me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful servant and a fellow slave in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am sending him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know how we are and he may encourage your hearts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He comes with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (you have received instructions about him: if he comes to you, welcome him),

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and so does Jesus who is called Justus. Of those from the circumcision, these alone are coworkers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ, greets you. He is always struggling for you in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I testify for him that he toils hard for you and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and Nympha and the assembly in her house.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the assembly of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the one from Laodicea.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “See to the service you received in the Lord, so that you fulfill it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

notes.note: The Greek word for the slave owners (“masters”) is the same word used for Jesus as “Lord.” The verse turns on that identity: those who own slaves are themselves under an owner. “Master” is used here to keep the echo audible.

The Greek noun can mean “equality” or “fairness, equity.” Most interpreters take it here as fair and even-handed treatment, a common sense in the period. A minority argue that Paul is calling for slaves to be treated as equals.

Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as a technical term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially God’s hidden plan that he alone discloses. “Secret” is used here because “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul’s point is that this is to be spoken and made plain.

notes.phrase: making the most of the time
notes.note: The verb is a marketplace term meaning to buy up or buy back. Most modern interpreters take it as seizing every opportunity, which is followed here. The older rendering “redeeming the time” assumes the idea of rescuing time from misuse. “Time” here is the word for an opportune moment, not for clock time.

Most versions have “fellow servant,” and “servant of Christ” for Epaphras in verse 12. The Greek word in both places is the ordinary term for a slave, the same used for the household slaves addressed in verse 1. A different word, rendered “servant,” stands beside it in this verse. Paul describes himself and his colleagues as owned by the Lord, and “slave” keeps that picture and the distinction between the two words.

The Greek verb is in a past tense, written from the viewpoint of the readers, for whom the sending would be past when the letter was read. Tychicus was almost certainly the bearer of the letter, so English idiom calls for the present. Some manuscripts read “that he may know how you are” in place of “that you may know how we are.”

This is generally identified with the Onesimus of the letter to Philemon, a slave from a Colossian household who is being sent back. If so, it is notable that Paul introduces him here simply as a faithful and beloved brother and “one of you.”

notes.phrase: Of those from the circumcision, these alone
notes.traditional: who are of the circumcision. These only are my fellow workers
notes.note: “Those from the circumcision” means Jews, here Jewish believers in Christ. The Greek can be punctuated to say either that these three are Jews and are Paul’s only coworkers, or that among his Jewish companions only these three work with him. The second is followed here and by most interpreters, since Paul goes on to name other coworkers who are evidently Gentiles.

notes.traditional: perfect and complete / mature and fully assured
notes.note: The first adjective can mean “perfect,” “complete” or “mature”; of persons in Paul it usually means grown-up, fully developed. The participle can mean either “fully convinced” or “filled, made complete.” The first is the more common sense of the verb in Paul and is followed here, while older versions have “complete.”

notes.phrase: Nympha and the assembly in her house
notes.note: “Church” is the near-universal rendering. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Scriptures’ term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. So “assembly” is used throughout this translation. The manuscripts differ over the name and pronoun: some have the woman Nympha and “her house,” others the man Nymphas and “his house,” and others “their house.” The feminine is followed here, as in most recent editions.

This is a letter that would reach Colossae by way of Laodicea, a neighboring city about ten miles away. Most scholars think it was a letter of Paul to the Laodiceans that has not survived. Others suggest it was the circular letter now known as Ephesians. The identification is uncertain.

Most versions have “ministry.” The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests a clerical profession. What Archippus’s task was is not known.

Letters were normally dictated to a secretary. The sender often added a closing line in his own handwriting as a personal touch and a mark of authenticity. Paul does the same at the end of several letters.

candidates.reason: This word and its compound σύνδουλος vary across versions between “slave,” “servant” and “bondservant,” and need one rendering to stay distinct from διάκονος, both for literal slaves and for “slave of Christ.”

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural, of the community); brother (singular, of a named man)
candidates.reason: The plural addressed to mixed communities recurs in every letter, and translators split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers.”
The Semitic idiom of “walking” for conduct recurs throughout Paul and John, and versions vary between “walk,” “live” and “conduct yourselves.”
Versions vary between “perfect,” “mature” and “complete” across Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and James, and the choice shapes how readers hear the demand.
This very frequent verb is rendered “encourage,” “comfort,” “urge,” “exhort” or “appeal” by different versions, and its senses need to be fixed consistently.
